source_text: Βασιλείδης δὲ ἐν τῷ εἰκοστῷ τρίτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸ μαρτύριον κολαζομένων αὐταῖς λέξεσι τάδε φησί· φημὶ γάρ τοι, ὁπόσοι ὑποπίπτουσι ταῖς λεγομέναις θλίψεσιν, ἤτοι ἡμαρτηκότες ἐν ἄλλοις λανθάνοντες πταίσμασιν εἰς τοῦτο ἄγονται τὸ ἀγαθόν, χρηστότητι τοῦ περιάγοντος ἄλλα ἐξ ἄλλων ὄντως ἐγκαλούμενοι, ἵνα μὴ ὡς κατάδικοι ἐπὶ κακοῖς ὁμολογουμένοις πάθωσι, μηδὲ λοιδορούμενοι ὡς ὁ μοιχὸς ἢ ὁ φονεύς, ἀλλ’ ὅτι Χριστιανοὶ † πεφυκότες, ὅπερ αὐτοὺς παρηγορήσει μηδὲ πάσχειν δοκεῖν· κἂν μὴ ἡμαρτηκὼς δ’ ὅλως τις ἐπὶ τὸ παθεῖν γένηται, σπάνιον μέν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ οὗτος κατ’ ἐπιβουλὴν δυνάμεώς τι πείσεται, ἀλλὰ πείσεται ὡς ἔπασχε καὶ τὸ νήπιον τὸ δοκοῦν οὐχ ἡμαρτηκέναι. εἶθ’ ὑποβὰς πάλιν ἐπιφέρει· ὡς οὖν τὸ νήπιον οὐ προημαρτηκὸς ἢ ἐνεργῶς μὲν οὐχ ἡμαρτηκὸς οὐδέν, ἐν ἑαυτῷ τῷ δὲ τὸ ἁμαρτῆσαι ἔχον, ἐπὰν ὑποβληθῇ τῷ παθεῖν, εὐεργετεῖται τε, πολλὰ κερδαῖνον δύσκολα, οὑτωσὶ δὴ κἂν τέλειος μηδὲν ἡμαρτηκὼς ἔργῳ τύχῃ, δέ, ἃν πάθῃ, τοῦτο ἔπαθεν ἐμφερῶς τῷ νηπίῳ· ἔχων μὲν γὰρ ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἁμαρτητικόν, ἀφορμὴν δὲ πρὸς τὸ ἡμαρτηκέναι μὴ λαβὼν οὐχ ἡμάρτανεν. ὥστ’ οὐκ αὐτῷ τὸ μὴ ἁμαρτῆσαι λογιστέον. ὡς γὰρ ὁ μοιχεῦσαι θέλων μοιχός ἐστι, κἂν τοῦ μοιχεῦσαι μὴ ἐπιτύχῃ, καὶ ὁ ποιῆσαι φόνον θέλων ἀνδροφόνος ἐστί, κἂν μὴ δύνηται φονεῦσαι, οὑτωσὶ δὴ καὶ τὸν ἀναμάρτητον ὃν λέγω ἐὰν ἴδω πάσχοντα, κἂν μηδὲν ᾖ κακὸν πεπραχώς, κακὸν ἐρῶ τῷ θέλειν ἁμαρτάνειν. πάντ’ ἐρῶ γὰρ μᾶλλον ἢ κακὸν τὸ προνοοῦν ἐρῶ. εἶθ’ ὑποβὰς καὶ περὶ τοῦ κυρίου ἄντικρυς ὡς περὶ ἀνθρώπου λέγει· ἐὰν μέντοι παραλιπὼν τούτους ἅπαντας τοὺς λόγους ἔλθῃς ἐπὶ τὸ δυσωπεῖν με διὰ προσώπων τινῶν, εἰ τύχοι, λέγων, ὁ δεῖνα οὖν ἥμαρτεν, ἔπαθεν γὰρ ὁ δεῖνα, ἐὰν μὲν ἐπιτρέπῃς, ἐρῶ, οὐχ ἥμαρτεν μέν, ὅμοιος δὲ ἦν τῷ πάσχοντι νηπίῳ· εἰ μέντοι σφοδρότερον ἐκβιάσαιο τὸν λόγον, ἐρῶ, ἄνθρωπον ὅντιν’ ἂν ὀνομάσῃς ἄνθρωπον εἶναι, δίκαιον δὲ τὸν θεόν. καθαρὸς γὰρ οὐδείς, ὥσπερ εἶπέ τις, ἀπὸ ῥύπου. ἀλλὰ τῷ Βασιλείδῃ ἡ ὑπόθεσις προαμαρτήσασάν φησι τὴν ψυχὴν ἐν ἑτέρῳ βίῳ τὴν κόλασιν ὑπομένειν ἐνταῦθα, τὴν μὲν ἐκλεκτὴν ἐπιτίμως διὰ μαρτυρίου, τὴν ἄλλην δὲ καθαιρομένην οἰκείᾳ κολάσει.
pass_a_gloss: Basilides says in the twenty-third of the Exegetical works concerning those punished according to the testimony that they suffer these things, for I say that as many as fall into the so-called afflictions, either having sinned in other hidden faults are led to this good, being truly accused of other things because of the kindness of the one leading them, so that they may not suffer as condemned for admitted evils, nor be reviled as the adulterer or the murderer, but because they have been made Christians, which will comfort them so that they do not seem to suffer. And even if someone has not sinned at all and comes to suffer, this is rare, but neither will he suffer by the force of power, but he will suffer as the innocent child suffers. Then he adds that just as the child is not a pre-sinner or actively a sinner, but has the ability to sin within himself, when he is subjected to suffering, he is benefited and gains much, even in difficult things. So also if a perfect person has not sinned in deed, but suffers, he suffers similarly to the child, for he has the sinful nature within himself, but has not taken the opportunity to sin. Therefore, it should not be reckoned to him that he did not sin. For just as the one who wants to commit adultery is an adulterer, even if he does not succeed in committing adultery, and the one who wants to commit murder is a murderer, even if he is not able to kill, so also I will say that the one who is without sin, if I see him suffering, even if he has not done anything evil, is evil in his willingness to sin. I will say that all things are more than evil, I will say that forethought is evil. Then he speaks also about the Lord, as if about a man, saying that if you leave all these words and come to calumniating me through certain persons, saying that so-and-so sinned and suffered, if you permit, I will say that he did not sin, but was like the suffering child. But if you force the argument more strongly, I will say that whoever you name as a man is a man, and God is just. For no one is pure, as someone has said, from filth. But Basilides' hypothesis says that the soul, having sinned beforehand in another life, endures punishment here, the elect suffering through martyrdom, the others being purified by their own punishment.

pass_b_english: Basilides writes in the twenty-third book of his *Exegetica* about those who are punished 'according to the testimony.' He says: 'I tell you that as many as fall into these so-called afflictions — whether they have sinned in other hidden faults and are led to this good, being truly accused of other things because of the kindness of the One who directs all things, so that they may not suffer as condemned for admitted evils, nor be reviled as the adulterer or the murderer, but because they have become Christians, which will comfort them so that they do not even seem to suffer — or even if someone has not sinned at all and yet comes to suffer (a rare case), neither will he suffer by the force of some power, but he will suffer as the innocent child suffers.'

He then adds: 'Just as the child is not a pre-sinner, or actively has not sinned in any deed, yet has the capacity to sin within himself, when he is subjected to suffering he is benefited and gains many things, even difficult ones. So also if a perfect person has not sinned in deed but suffers, he suffers similarly to the child; for he has the sinful nature within himself, but has not taken the opportunity to sin. Therefore, it should not be reckoned to him that he did not sin. For just as the one who wants to commit adultery is an adulterer, even if he does not succeed in committing adultery, and the one who wants to commit murder is a murderer, even if he is not able to kill, so also I will say that the one who is without sin, if I see him suffering, even if he has not done anything evil, is evil in his willingness to sin. I will say that all things are more than evil; I will say that forethought itself is evil.'

Then he speaks also about the Lord, as if about a mere man: 'If, however, you leave all these arguments and come to calumniating me through certain persons, saying, "So-and-so sinned, for so-and-so suffered," if you permit, I will say, "He did not sin, but was like the suffering child." But if you force the argument more strongly, I will say, "Whoever you name as a man is a man, and God is just. For no one is pure from filth, as someone has said."' But Basilides' hypothesis asserts that the soul, having sinned beforehand in another life, endures punishment here: the elect worthily through martyrdom, the others being purified by their own punishment.
